articles.headline: OFAC Designates New Entities and Individuals in Latest Iran-Related Sanctions
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations on November 6, 2026. This action targets individuals and entities involved in activities supporting the Iranian regime.

These designations are part of ongoing efforts to counter Iran's destabilizing activities and its pursuit of illicit financing networks. Further details regarding the specific individuals and entities, and the nature of their involvement, are available on the Treasury's website.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes Cyber-related and Transnational Criminal Organization Sanctions, Designates Cuban Entities
body: On November 5, 2026, OFAC issued new designations targeting cyber-related activities and transnational criminal organizations. Concurrently, new sanctions were imposed on entities connected to Cuba.

This action also included the publication of a Cuba-related determination, further tightening restrictions on certain sectors of the Cuban economy. The designations aim to disrupt illicit networks and pressure the Cuban regime.
The Cuba-related determination specifically applies to the electronics, manufacturing, marine, and technology sectors of the Cuban economy, effective November 5, 2026.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues New Iran Sanctions, Updates Listings, and Amends Venezuela General License
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations and updates to existing listings on November 4, 2026. This action is accompanied by the publication of an Iran-related OFAC Alert titled "Iranian Shadow Fleet Reliance on False Flags for Sanctions Evasion."

Additionally, OFAC issued an amended Venezuela-related General License 5AA, which authorizes certain transactions related to the Petróleos de Venezuela, S.A. 2020 8.5 Percent Bond on or after December 18, 2026.

The Iran-related alert highlights the significant risk of designation or penalties for providing services to vessels that use false flags to evade U.S. sanctions on Iran, emphasizing the use of fraudulent registries and falsely claimed flags.

articles.headline: OFAC Amends Iran-Related General License
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) issued an amended Iran-related General License on October 29, 2026. This amendment modifies existing authorizations concerning transactions involving Iran.
The specific details of the changes are available on the OFAC website and are intended to refine the scope of permissible activities under the Iran sanctions program.

articles.region: North Korea, Democratic Republic of the Congo
articles.headline: OFAC Designates Entities and Individuals Linked to North Korea and DRC
body: On October 28, 2026, the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new designations targeting individuals and entities connected to North Korea and the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC).

These actions aim to disrupt illicit networks supporting North Korea's weapons programs and to address corruption and human rights abuses in the DRC. The specific targets and the reasons for their designation are detailed in the official announcement.

articles.headline: Extreme Networks Settles with OFAC for $1.5 Million Over Russia Sanctions Violations
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced a $1,529,685 settlement with Extreme Networks, Inc. on October 27, 2026.

The settlement resolves nine apparent violations of the Ukraine-/Russia-Related Sanctions Regulations. Between September 2018 and March 2022, Extreme Networks exported networking equipment and services to a Russian defense manufacturer, JSC Moskovskiy Mashinostroitelniy Zavod Avangard (MMZA), which was majority-owned by a designated entity, JSC Concern Almaz Antey, and thus blocked by operation of law.

OFAC determined that the apparent violations were egregious but voluntarily self-disclosed. The Department of Justice also announced a parallel non-prosecution agreement with Extreme Networks, involving criminal penalties totaling over $900,000.

articles.headline: OFAC Amends FAQs on Blocking, Rejecting Transactions, and Reporting
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) issued amendments to several Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs) on October 26, 2026. These updates pertain to guidance on blocking and rejecting transactions, as well as filing reports with OFAC.

The revisions clarify existing policies and procedures, ensuring that financial institutions and other entities have current information regarding their obligations under U.S. sanctions programs. The amended FAQs cover topics such as which jurisdictions are broadly sanctioned, how to block an account or funds transfer, and the timing and procedures for reporting blocked property and rejected transactions.

articles.headline: OFAC Designates Iran-Related Entities, Removes Belarus and North Korea Listings, Issues New GLs
body: On October 21, 2026, the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations. Concurrently, OFAC removed certain entities and individuals from its Belarus and North Korea sanctions lists.

Additionally, OFAC issued new Iran-related and Russia-related General Licenses and amended several Frequently Asked Questions. The removals from the Belarus and North Korea sanctions lists include Chinese national Lu Hezheng and two Chinese entities, as well as Belarusian national Andrei Alekseevich Rybakov.
These actions reflect a dynamic approach to sanctions, adjusting to evolving geopolitical landscapes and specific compliance considerations.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues Designations Under Protecting American Intellectual Property Act of 2022 (PAIPA)
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new designations under the Protecting American Intellectual Property Act of 2022 (PAIPA) on October 19, 2026. These designations are accompanied by the issuance of associated General Licenses.

This action targets individuals and entities involved in the theft or misappropriation of American intellectual property, underscoring the U.S. government's commitment to safeguarding innovation and economic security.

articles.headline: OFAC Amends Venezuela-Related General License and FAQ
body: On October 16, 2026, the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) issued an amended Venezuela-related General License and an updated Frequently Asked Question (FAQ).
The General License 60A, "Authorizing Transactions Related to Earthquake Relief Efforts in Venezuela," aims to facilitate humanitarian aid.
Additionally, OFAC issued one amended Frequently Asked Question, FAQ 1263, to provide further clarity on the scope and application of the Venezuela sanctions program.

articles.headline: Extreme Networks, Inc. Pays $1,529,685 to Settle OFAC Sanctions Violations
body: Extreme Networks, Inc. has agreed to pay $1,529,685 to the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) to settle apparent violations of U.S. sanctions regulations.

The settlement addresses nine apparent violations of the Ukraine-/Russia-Related Sanctions Regulations, involving the export of networking equipment and services to a Russian defense manufacturer that was a blocked person.
OFAC determined that the violations were egregious but voluntarily self-disclosed, leading to the agreed-upon penalty amount.

articles.headline: Bank of America, N.A. Fined $11,662,930 by OFAC for Sanctions Breaches
body: Bank of America, N.A. has been assessed a civil monetary penalty of $11,662,930 by the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) for 475 apparent violations of various U.S. sanctions programs.
The violations, which occurred between September 2021 and April 2025, involved transactions related to Russia, Belarus, Iran, Burma, Somalia, narcotics, and global terrorism.
This penalty was part of a coordinated enforcement action by the U.S. Treasury Department, which also included significant fines from FinCEN and the OCC for anti-money laundering failures.

articles.headline: Pegasus Worldwide Logistics Pays $175,015 for OFAC Sanctions Violations
body: Pegasus Worldwide Logistics has agreed to pay $175,015 to the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) to settle apparent violations of U.S. sanctions regulations.
The specific details of the violations are outlined in the settlement agreement, highlighting the importance of robust compliance programs for logistics companies engaged in international trade.

body: Rice Lake Weighing Systems, Inc. has agreed to pay $60,764 to the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) to resolve apparent violations of U.S. sanctions regulations.
The settlement highlights the need for all companies, regardless of size or industry, to implement effective sanctions compliance programs to prevent inadvertent breaches.

articles.headline: Adani Enterprises Limited Fined $275,000,000 by OFAC

This substantial penalty underscores the global reach of U.S. sanctions and the critical importance of compliance for international corporations, particularly those with complex supply chains and diverse business operations.

articles.headline: Individual Fined $3,777,000 by OFAC for Syrian Sanctions Violations
body: An individual has been assessed a civil monetary penalty of $3,777,000 by the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) for 20 apparent violations of the Syrian Sanctions Regulations.

The violations occurred between 2018 and 2021 and involved a U.S. citizen residing abroad. This substantial penalty underscores OFAC's focus on enforcing sanctions against individuals who facilitate prohibited transactions.

articles.headline: IMG Academy, LLC Settles with OFAC for $1,720,000 Over Kingpin Act Violations
body: IMG Academy, LLC has agreed to pay $1,720,000 to the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) to settle apparent violations of the Foreign Narcotics Kingpin Sanctions Regulations.

Over a five-year period, IMG Academy entered into tuition enrollment agreements and processed 89 related financial transactions for the benefit of children of two individuals designated under the Kingpin Act.

OFAC highlighted that routine due diligence, such as screening contracting parties or payors, would have revealed the individuals' names matched entries on the SDN List, emphasizing the need for academic institutions to implement robust sanctions compliance programs.

articles.headline: Streamlining Export Controls for Drone Exports
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is easing export controls on certain Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs or drones) and related parts, components, accessories, attachments, technology, and software under the Export Administration Regulations (EAR). Specifically, this rule: eliminates wind gust tolerance as a parameter for determining UAV controls under the EAR; increases the threshold for national security controls on certain UAVs from an endurance of 30 minutes to an endurance of 3 hours; makes conforming changes to remove national security controls on software and technology associated with UAVs with an endurance less than 3 hours; maintains military end-use and end-user controls on those lower endurance drones and associated software and technology; clarifies Commerce Control List (CCL) controls for certain UAVs specially designed for military use; and removes national security controls on certain specially designed parts, components, accessories, and attachments for such UAVs as they do not provide any significant military or intelligence capabilities.
